1:
The date is the chapter's great crux. Clarke sets out more than a dozen chronologists, from Glycas at 330 years to Serarius at 680, and concludes that the common Hebrew text is as likely to be right as any of them. Ellicott defends the verse against the charge of interpolation, explaining the Septuagint's 440 as an interchange of two similar Hebrew letters and Josephus's 592 as a tacit harmony with some heathen reckoning, and arguing that a date disagreeing at first sight with the earlier indications is the last thing a scribe would insert. Gill and Henry do not argue but reckon, adding the wilderness, Joshua, the judges, Eli, Samuel and Saul, David and Solomon's four years to the total.

On the measurements Ellicott sees a pattern the others miss: the temple copies the tabernacle with each dimension doubled, and so eight times its cubical contents, yet still small, not larger than a good-sized parish church, and in plan oddly like a Gothic one, a resemblance he lays to the old Freemasonry that took Solomon's plan for a sacred guide. Henry notes the doubling too, provision for a people grown both more numerous and richer. Clarke reduces the cubits to yards, feet and inches on Cumberland's figure, then declines to describe the building at all, since men professing the same principles produced very different ones. Delitzsch rejects the hundred and twenty cubits assigned the porch in 2 Chronicles 3:4, against Ewald and Stieglitz who defend it, since no such erection could be called a hall.

The windows divide them four ways over what the Hebrew allows. Henry takes them broad within and narrow without and draws a moral, that our minds should look much within to judge ourselves and little without to censure our brethren; the narrow lights intimated the darkness of that dispensation. Clarke reads them as latticed, open within and shut without, notes we hear nothing of glass, and hazards that window was once windore, a door to let the wind in. Delitzsch denies the received gloss outright: the phrase means windows with closed beams, fixed lattices that could not be opened at pleasure, though he allows the Chaldee tradition accords with the fact if not with the words. Ellicott grants the splayed reading good authorities but prefers the fixed lattices, immovable so none could look out or in.

The stones made ready before they were brought draw the warmest comment. Henry makes it a rule of prudence out of Proverbs 24:27 and then a lesson, that quietness and silence both become and befriend religious exercises, setting against it the psalm where the destroyers roared in the congregation: clamour and violence often hinder God's work but never further it. Clarke asks why the point is so particularly marked and answers that the temple was a type, the stones squared and fitted here for their place in the New Jerusalem. Ellicott calls the provision one of reverence, suspects the prohibition of tools on the altar suggested it though the idea there was different, and quotes Heber's lines on the noiseless fabric springing like some tall palm. Delitzsch settles the philology: the stones were not unhewn but so perfectly tooled in the quarry that no iron was required at the building.

The side building is technical and there Delitzsch is nearly the whole commentary: the outwork ran round the two long sides and the back, not the front, its three stories widening from five cubits to seven because rebates cut in the temple wall carried their beams, so nothing was inserted into the wall itself, and the whole stood twelve or fourteen cubits short of the house, leaving room for the windows. Henry says what the chambers were for, vestries where the utensils were laid up and the priests dressed, and warns that the church's strength should not be impaired under pretence of adding to its beauty.
11:
Nothing in the text says how the word reached Solomon, and the gap is filled differently. Gill follows the Targum in calling it a word of prophecy and allows either an impulse of the Spirit or the hand of a prophet, noting that Kimchi prefers the second and that some Jewish writers name Ahijah the Shilonite as the messenger. Delitzsch reasons from the phrasing: that the word of the Lord came seems to point to a prophetic medium, and this agrees with the later notice that God revealed himself to Solomon by an actual appearance only twice. Clarke takes up a different question, whether this is the same revelation as the one recorded after the dedication. Some think it is; to him it appears different, a word given while the building was going forward, to encourage him, to warn him against apostasy, and to assure him of continued protection if he and his family remained faithful to the grace given them.

Delitzsch is alone on the construction. The house is placed at the head absolutely, so the sense runs as for the house which thou art building, if thou walkest in my statutes, then I will set up my word; and the word in question is the promise of an everlasting throne made in 2 Samuel 7:12. On that reading the assurance that follows, that God will dwell among the children of Israel, adds no second promise but applies the old one to the building now begun. Henry hears it rather as a widening, the divine loving-kindness drawn out both to Solomon himself in the performing of the word and to his kingdom in the dwelling and the not forsaking.

On why the message came in the middle of the work all four converge, and Henry gives it most fully, in two parts. First for encouragement: the great care, expense and fatigue might well have made Solomon wish he had never begun, and an eye to the promise will carry a man cheerfully through his work. Second for admonition: the condition annexed was there to make him consider that he might build the temple ever so strong and its glory would still depart unless he and his people continued to walk in God's statutes, since all that charge would neither excuse them from obedience to the law nor shelter them from judgment in case of disobedience. Gill reaches the same point through Abarbinel, that the message came in the midst of the work to keep Solomon from depending on the strength of the fabric, its perpetuity hanging on his own conduct and his successors' and the people's; conscious of his integrity and hoping well of posterity, he was not discouraged but carried the work to perfection.

Henry then draws the sharpest sentence in the chapter, that keeping God's commandments is better and more pleasing to him than building churches, and adds that none employ themselves for God without having his eye upon them, since the message opens by taking notice of the work in hand. He makes something of the bare statement that Solomon built the house and finished it: the strictness of God's government will never drive a good man from his service but quicken him in it, and Solomon proceeded on those terms, meeting none of the obstructions that later stopped the work at Jerusalem, neither out-building his property nor doing the thing by halves, because he was a wise builder. Gill reads the same statement as animation, Solomon going on until he had completed it, encouraged by the promise of the divine presence provided a proper regard was had to the will and ways of God.
15:
On the lining Delitzsch thinks the text has slipped: walls of the ceiling is very striking and probably a copyist's error for beams of the ceiling. The whole inside was covered with wood, so nothing of the stone wall was seen. Ellicott prefers the marginal reading, agreeing with the Greek and the Latin, that from the floor to the walls of the ceiling all was cedar and the floor laid with cypress. Henry attends to the material, cedar being strong, durable and of a very sweet smell, and to the wainscot, carved with knops like eggs or apples, and flowers, no doubt as the fashion then was.

The name of the inner room is a real dispute. Henry and Gill take it as settled, the oracle or speaking-place, for so the word signifies, because thence God spoke to Moses and, Henry adds, perhaps to the high priest consulting the breastplate of judgment. Delitzsch reports it as contested: Aquila and Symmachus rendered it a place of responses and the Latin oraculum, deriving it from the verb to speak, which Hengstenberg adopts, but most recent commentators follow a different lead.

The forepart of the oracle divides them, and on Gill's reading it changes the building. Ellicott grants that in the forepart is literal but holds the sense clearly to be in the inner part, as the Latin renders it, and cites Gesenius for taking the word properly of the wall facing the entrance, and thence of the inner region. Delitzsch reaches the same place by grammar, agreeing with Kimchi that the form is the construct of a noun meaning the interior. Gill keeps the plain English and builds on it: the forepart is what stood before a man's face as he entered, and since twenty cubits of height leave ten unaccounted for, he supposes the back part rose to the full thirty while the forepart was lower and open, to let in the light of the candlesticks and the smoke of the incense.

On the gold Gill alone puts a figure to it, six hundred talents, or something over three million pounds sterling, where Clarke says flatly that it is impossible to calculate the expense. Henry notes that the gilding was not washed over like ours but laid on the whole house, then turns it round: gold was under foot there, as it should be in all the living temples, the abundance of it lessening its worth. Delitzsch worries the adjective instead, fine gold, whose derivation he leaves questionable, whether from shutting up, so gold carefully preserved, or from selecting, so gold that is pure.

The chains before the oracle defeat both grammarians. Delitzsch calls the words very obscure, withdraws his earlier view that the house meant the party wall, and follows Gesenius and de Wette in taking the verb in the Chaldee sense of bolting or fastening. Ellicott notes that the Greek and the Latin have wholly different readings, judges our translation substantially correct, and offers a choice between a chain-work decoration on the partition and, more probably, a golden chain across the entrance before the veil, a guard against intrusion. On the altar he is sharper: at the earlier verse our translators were misled by the context into anticipating the gilding, when the meaning is that Solomon covered the altar, presumably of stone, with cedar. The altar belonging to the oracle he explains carefully: it is the altar of incense, standing before the veil and so in the holy place, yet reckoned to belong in idea to the holy of holies, since offering incense signified approach to the unseen presence and taking the censer from it was the condition of entering on the day of atonement. That is why Exodus 40:5 sets it before the ark, and probably why the Epistle to the Hebrews gives the holiest place the altar of incense, wrongly rendered censer in our version.
23:
Whether the wood was olive is the first small question. Gill notes that the phrase is oil tree and that pine and cypress yield oil too, which some think are meant, though the Targum says olive; Delitzsch takes it for the oleaster or wild olive, very firm and durable. Gill then lists the differences from the pair Moses made: these were larger, of olive wood rather than gold, and stood on the floor instead of rising at the two ends of the mercy seat and made out of it. Henry explains why they were needed at all, the most holy place being much larger than in the tabernacle, so the ark would have seemed lost in it and the dead wall unsightly unadorned. Clarke contributes the height in modern measure, about eighteen feet and three inches.

What they looked like is a real question and Ellicott presses it. The cherubim over the ark, he observes, are described in only three places in the Old Testament besides the visions of Ezekiel, which determined the imagery of the Apocalypse, and in no case is their form distinctly mentioned; it may perhaps be inferred to have been a winged bull by comparing two passages in Ezekiel, whence the golden calves of the later idolatry would naturally derive. Against this he sets Josephus, who says expressly that no one can tell or even conjecture what shape they were, and concludes that the tradition must have been lost in the second temple, where there was no ark, which he finds stranger because cherubim were embroidered on the curtains and carved on these walls. Delitzsch has no such hesitation, giving them a human form like the golden cherubs on the ark and setting them upright on their feet; Henry says images of young men, as some think.

On what they signify Ellicott is fullest, and he begins negatively: whatever they were, they were in no sense representations or emblems of Deity, like the winged figures of Assyria or Egypt with which they have often been compared. They appear to him rather to symbolise the great physical forces of the universe, guided by superhuman angelic intelligence to serve the supreme will of God, and he traces it through the flaming sword that guarded the tree of life, the Lord riding upon the cherubim in Psalm 18:10, the living creatures bearing away the throne in Ezekiel, and the same creatures joining the elders in worship in the Revelation. Their presence in the temple, on this reading, simply claims for the God of Israel the lordship over all creation that the seraphic song of Isaiah 6:3 hymns.

Henry and Gill read them as persons rather than forces. Henry sets them against the heathen practice: the heathen set up images of their gods and worshipped them, but these represent the servants and attendants of the God of Israel, the holy angels, not to be themselves worshipped but to show how great he is whom we are to worship. Gill allows the angelic reading, the angels in their greatness and glory, always in God's presence, beholding his face and waiting to do his will, but prefers another, that the two figures stand for the two witnesses who are called the two olive trees standing before the God of the whole earth; and carries it into the gilding, which may denote the purity and excellency of angels or the gifts and graces adorning the witnesses. Ellicott meanwhile draws a conclusion from the wings: since they stretch across the room and touch the walls, the figures must have faced the entrance, where in the tabernacle they faced the mercy seat, and he suggests the change of attitude denoted a change of idea characteristic of Solomon and his age, the old attitude clearly one of worship of God and the new rather of manifestation of his glory to man.
29:
Ellicott alone asks how far the carving went. Taken literally, the cherubim and palm trees covered all the walls; otherwise one might have supposed them confined to the oracle within and the partition without, which would seem more appropriate, the cherubim belonging especially to the oracle. Gill reads the ornament instead: if the cherubim stand for angels, the palm trees fitly represent just and upright men, who appear in the church below and in heaven above, where the open flowers of divine grace are also seen.

The gilding gets closer attention than the carving. Delitzsch explains that gold leaf was spread so that, as Rashi observes, every elevation and depression of the carving was impressed on the coating and plainly seen, and notes that ancient gilding was generally done by laying on gold plate fastened with tacks. Thenius inferred from that clause that the gilding was confined to the engraved figures and did not cover the whole walls and doors; Delitzsch calls the inference very doubtful. Ellicott finds the description minutely accurate in another way: on the oracle doors the gold was spread, covering the carvings in relief, while on the outer doors it was fitted, beaten into shape over the carved work.

The doors are where Delitzsch fights hardest. The words about the posts being a fifth are obscure and have been read in very different ways; he holds they can hardly mean anything but that the projecting framework occupied a fifth of the wall's breadth, and rejects the alternative of posts of a fifth thickness, which has no support in Ezekiel and requires an unwarranted sense for one word and a wall two cubits thick. Ellicott turns the same figures into dimensions, four cubits for lintel and post, so each oracle door was less than six feet by three, and notes that they stood open as a rule, showing the veil and the golden chains. For the outer doors, a fourth of the wall, he explains that because they were heavier and oftener opened each leaf was made to fold again upon itself. Delitzsch adds the reason for the change of wood: cypress was chosen for the holy place rather than olive, probably as lighter and so less likely to sink.

The court divides them over whether a floor or a wall is described. Ellicott sets out both, either a floor raised by three courses of stone and covered with cedar planking, or, as Josephus understands it, an enclosure of three courses with a cedar coping. He prefers the second, since the altar and the laver stood there and all the sacrifices went on, which could hardly be done on a wooden pavement. Clarke takes the words as alternating courses running all through the wall, three of stone and one of timber, and asks whether such a building could be durable; he observes that the palace was built the same way, so this was probably the ordinary manner for better buildings, notes that Calmet refers the stone crying out of the wall and the beam answering it in Habakkuk 2:11 to this mode, and adds that here the timber was at least not exposed.

Delitzsch and Henry arrive independently at the same explanation of the low wall. Delitzsch, having identified the inner court as the priests' and inferred an outer one, notes that Jeremiah calls it the upper court, so it stood higher, and suggests the cedar beams may have been set upright as palisading so the people could see through into the priests' court. Henry says the same without the philology and draws the lesson: the low wall of three rows of hewn stone tipped with a cornice of cedar was so that over it the people might see what was done and hear what the priests said, for even under that dispensation they were not kept wholly in the dark or at a distance.
37:
The two month-names get different etymologies. Ellicott glosses Zif as the brightness of flowers, about May, and Bul as the month of rain, about November. Delitzsch takes Bul instead from a word for produce, making it the fruit month, and supposes the name came from the Phoenicians, with whom fruit ripened later, and is said to be found on the great Sidonian inscription. Clarke simply places Zif in April and May and Bul in October and November.

Whether seven years and a half is fast or slow divides them. Clarke finds it rather strange that the house needed so long, since the stones and timbers were prepared before they came to Jerusalem, and resolves it by the ornamenting, gilding and carved work, which must have consumed considerable time; he notes too that the round seven is properly seven years and six months, Scripture generally expressing things in round numbers. Delitzsch and Henry think the opposite. Delitzsch says that compared with other large buildings of antiquity and of modern times the work was done in a very short time, and Henry, allowing for the vastness and elegance of the building and all its appurtenances, says it was soon done: Solomon was in earnest, had money enough, had nothing to divert him, and many hands made quick work.

Clarke and Delitzsch reach independently for the same comparison, both citing Pliny on the temple of Diana at Ephesus, at which all Asia was building for two centuries. Clarke adds that it was certainly more extensive, and that it may justly be questioned whether Solomon's temple, for all its profusion of gold and precious stones, cost anything like Diana's, and that the men employed twenty years on an Egyptian pyramid are no measure of it. What follows is his best observation: the temple was never intended to hold a vast concourse of people, the courts and chambers being far more extensive than the temple itself, so it was never designed as a place to worship in but a place to worship at, the priests alone employed within and the tribes coming before God without.

Clarke declines to describe the building and prints an account borrowed from Calmet, whose governing argument is worth keeping: the writers of Kings and Chronicles describe the temple properly so called but scarcely the courts and open areas, which made a principal part of the grandeur; Ezekiel supplied the defect. Ezekiel's temple was never restored on his model after the captivity, but since his measures for the sanctum and sanctuary are within a small matter the same, and he was a priest who had seen the first house, his plan is taken to stand for Solomon's. One discrepancy is left standing: Ezekiel makes the side chambers four cubits wide where this chapter allows five, six and seven. It also settles the forty-six years of John 2:20, which do not mean that Herod spent forty-six years, since Josephus says he finished in nine and a half, the additions going on to the beginning of the Jewish war.

Henry closes with what the house was a type of, in four stages. Christ is the true temple, who spoke of the temple of his body, in whom dwelt the fulness of the Godhead as the glory dwelt here. Every believer is a living temple, built on Christ and perfected in due time. The gospel church is the mystical temple, and here Henry presses the architecture: only Jews built the tabernacle, but Gentiles joined in building the temple, and the door into the house was wider than the door into the oracle, many entering into profession who come short of salvation. Heaven is the everlasting temple, its streets pure gold in allusion to this flooring, and there, as here, no noise of axes, all who will be stones in that building having to be hewn and squared by divine grace beforehand.
